facts: NBS Circular 592 reports that molybdenum-bearing stainless-steel types 316 and 317 were the most resistant to sulfuric acid at low temperatures.

The Circular states that at about 150° F all of the stainless steels corrode in practically all concentrations of acid up to 95 percent (the scanned page shows the upper bound '95 percent' but the lower concentration bound in the phrase is OCR-corrupted and not legible).
Roach and Hall (cited in the Circular) reported that molybdenum-bearing stainless steels were useful, at room temperature, in concentrations of sulfuric acid below 15 percent and above 85 percent.
The Circular says resistance to sulfuric acid is improved in some cases by additions of copper or cerium.

The Circular warns that hydrochloric acid and some solutions containing halide ions attack the passive film on stainless steel and produce pitting; additions of molybdenum reduce susceptibility to pitting corrosion.

The severity of corrosion and stress-corrosion cracking varies with composition, corrosive medium, temperature, tensile stresses, and other factors; stress plus exposure can produce stress-corrosion cracking.
Incomplete removal of residual welding flux or other fabrication issues can initiate rapid corrosion or change corrosion resistance.

The Circular’s statements are based on cited studies (e.g., Kiefer & Renshaw; Roach & Hall) and specific test/field conditions; therefore the reported ranking is an empirical observation under particular conditions and not a universal material recommendation.
